Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages . The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action. Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images "We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments. The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase , an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple . On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation-state." He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee. "We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor." But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame. The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported." Sen. Mark Warner , D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC on Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety. "I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm." His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO. Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry." He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like the Hugging Face breach earlier this year. — CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report. headlines.article_text: Lowe's (LOW) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year. The home improvement retailer said it's also seeing strength among its professional shoppers. The company said it received roughly $250 million in tariff benefits during the quarter. In this article LOW Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:58 06:58 Lowe’s posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market Squawk Box Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers. The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion. Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years. "We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC. Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers. He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects. "We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program." Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted vs. $2.88 expected Revenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior. The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter. "So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said. Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far. Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.
